tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Case Study: A Speed-Adjusted Receiver Grade and the Landry, Kupp and Brown Examples

**What it is** — Eric Eager (PFF) wanted to put in-game speed (the miles-per-hour figures shown at events such as the Senior Bowl) in the context of PFF's receiving grade: can a receiver turn speed into a good grade, meaning catching the ball in stride, not dropping or misjudging it (Q3i3FOC-dPE [12:54], [13:25]). He built a model with mean, median and max speed over the play. His report: speed is "the most important variable" for a positive grade on go and corner routes (caption "an eight or nine route"), though other factors also matter (Q3i3FOC-dPE [13:25], [13:55]). The resulting adjusted grade is more correlated with itself year to year than the deep-pass grade, and correlates with the 40-yard dash (Q3i3FOC-dPE [13:55], [14:25]). Examples: Jarvis Landry, a good receiver since 2014, had a quite slow 40, and Cooper Kupp (caption "cooper cup") was much faster in games than his 4.62, which Eager thinks was his pro day in 2017 (he was unsure of the year) (Q3i3FOC-dPE [14:25], [14:56]). In Q&A he explains Antonio Brown (sixth-round pick, ran poorly at the combine) as playing fast with ball control: the measure captures running fast "in a controlled way" enough to make football plays (Q3i3FOC-dPE [20:28], [21:30]).

**Why it works** — Eager's account: players who play fast on the field generally test fast, but there is enough noise to find players who cannot translate off-field speed to on-field functional speed (Q3i3FOC-dPE [14:25]). He gives no mechanism for the exceptions beyond resources and body control. Inference: Brown's low test and high speed rank would partly reflect trainers and test preparation, which Eager raises as a possible reason (Q3i3FOC-dPE [20:28], [20:59]).

**When to apply** — Use the three examples as the questions to ask when comparing test speed with game speed. Inference: if Catapult (documented in the Applied Performance playbook as the GPS device) provides game max velocity and a graded outcome is available per player, line them up for one position group and look before modeling. Eric's baseline: no formal sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist: "They do not exist formally" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7).

**When NOT to apply** — Single named players, no group-level numbers in the captions beyond the year-to-year claim, and the correlation with the 40 is not quantified at this point (Q3i3FOC-dPE [14:25]). `untested`. Tracking data is NFL-wide. A grade is a human judgment: the speaker says the graders pick among half-point steps and are not asked to do context math (Q3i3FOC-dPE [26:36], [27:07]). Do not use speed alone to predict receiver quality.

**Example** — The speaker's, above (Landry, Kupp, Brown).

**Related** — [[heuristic--time-varying-athleticism-instead-of-one-combine-number]], [[framework--charted-grades-as-labels-tracking-data-as-predictors]], [[framework--open-score-orientation-speed-trajectory-before-release]], another receiver metric that refuses to equate speed or distance with success.

# Combining Ability and Stress Tolerance Predicted Coach-Rated Decisions Under Stress, and Related to Penalties

**What it is** — The first speaker (caption spelling "Ken yuso") reports that intelligence and personality combined predict some coach ratings better than either alone (overall about 0.35, 40NV3_u9tYY [15:33]). The example is decision-making under stress: combining the intelligence score with the personality stress-tolerance variable gave "a 0.22 correlation" (caption "a0 22") with the coaches' rating of decisions under stress (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03]). His reasoning: a calm player who decides badly does not help, so the interesting question is whether a player continues to decide well under stress (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03], [16:35]). Moving to on-field metrics, this variable "actually correlating with penalties" per play and yards per penalty, standardized across position, with better results for defensive backs ("Dbacks", caption) than across all positions (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35], [17:07]). A larger second sample of about 400 players held the result (40NV3_u9tYY [17:07]). The size of the penalty correlations is not stated aloud ("a pretty nice correlation").

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that decisions under stress need both the cognitive ability to decide well and the personality trait to stay composed (40NV3_u9tYY [16:03], [16:35]). No further mechanism is given. Inference: the combination result is an interaction or additive effect, and the talk does not say which.

**When to apply** — As a model for a measurement design: define the behavior of interest (decide well under pressure), then see which measured traits jointly predict it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: for Baylor, a question like "who stays accurate when fatigued or loaded" would have to be defined first, with its own criterion.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: 0.22 is the only value given, the penalty correlations have no stated size, and no intervals or position-level results are shown. Penalties are influenced by position, scheme and officiating, which the speaker's "standardize across position" does not remove. The outcome in the main result is coach opinion of decisions, not measured decisions. The finding is for NFL rookies and early-career players on one test, not a general rule for college athletes or for Baylor.

**Example** — The talk's: a calm, cool player who makes lousy decisions versus one who keeps deciding well under stress, with the second the target (40NV3_u9tYY [16:35]).

**Related** — [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]], [[claim--personality-scores-relate-weakly-to-injury]].

# In Fatigued Pitchers the Velocity-Stress Link Broke Down

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group put pitchers through a simulated seven-inning game and asked for a fatigue rating from 1 to 10 after each inning (z_6M5r7031A [05:10]). The ratings rose inning by inning. Peak fastball velocity began to dip around inning five, "not that surprising" to him (z_6M5r7031A [05:10] to [05:40]). What surprised the group: when elbow stress should have come down with the lower velocity, it went up. Compared with pitchers who were not fatigued, "the velocity-stress relationship totally broke down" in fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]). The sample size is not stated, and the talk says the study was done "recently."

His hypothesis, offered in Q&A: throwing starts from the toes, back and core, and as those muscles fatigue while the pitcher tries to hold velocity, "the arm's doing everything" (z_6M5r7031A [24:11]). For a 13-year-old's parents he suggests core and bodyweight exercises such as planks, not heavy lifting, and says his group will start looking into this (z_6M5r7031A [24:11] to [24:42]).

**Why it works** — The kinetic-chain account above is the speaker's hypothesis, not a tested result. He illustrates it with his own tennis serve (z_6M5r7031A [23:40] to [24:11]). The simulated-game study did not measure the other body segments in anything the talk reports.

**When to apply** — As a prompt to check whether an output (velocity, jump height, sprint speed) still holds while a driver or strategy metric changes late in a session or week. Eric's baseline: force-plate reporting picks output, driver and strategy metrics (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics, not Eric's own framework; hd-odsf-metrics.md). Inference: this finding is an example of output alone misleading, since the velocity looked acceptable while the stress rose. Eric's baseline: bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk and comes before loaded work (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this matches the speaker's planks-over-heavy-lifting advice for a young athlete, though the speaker's advice is about a 13-year-old.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one simulated-game study, sample size not stated, no numbers shown for stress or velocity, and the mechanism is a hypothesis. It was pitchers in a simulated game, not a competition. Do not conclude that stress rises with fatigue in other sports or movements. Do not use the kinetic-chain idea to prescribe training; the speaker says he is only starting to study it.

**Example** — The speaker's own: velocity dips at inning five, yet stress rises instead of falling, unlike non-fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the relationship that broke down).

# The Mid-Range Share Fell, but Stars' Self-Created Mid-Range Shots Held Steady

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Seth part now") tests "the mid-range game has been lost". He defines mid-range as outside the paint and inside the three-point arc (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:43]). Part true: the mid-range share "plummeted" while the three-point share rose, which is "unmistakably true" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [08:43], [09:14]). Part not: when people mourn the lost mid-range, he argues they mean players creating their own shot at the top of the key or elbows, not a power forward taking a 17-foot baseline jump shot (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:14]).
- Unassisted (self-created) mid-range shots "have held basically steady" over time as a proportion of mid-range shots (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:44]); assisted catch-and-shoot attempts moved from low-value areas toward the rim and the corners (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:14]).
- For high-usage players, defined arbitrarily as usage 27% or higher, long two-pointers rose from 7% to 11.5% of their made shots over about 15 years, "over 50%" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:44]).
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by this group doubled to tripled over four years, driven by a few players; about 340 extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate, of which two players accounted for 308, "if I did the math correctly" (BJkCqf6Fj2w [11:16], [11:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is a redefinition of what "mid-range" means in the complaint, which he calls "star shots" taken by the best players (BJkCqf6Fj2w [09:44]). No mechanism is given for why stars' share held steady.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to split an aggregate trend by who produces the shots (assisted or not, usage group) before accepting a story. Inference: the same split applies to team-level load or testing averages that hide a few athletes who drive the change; at Baylor, check the athlete-level distribution before reading a team trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Supported for the direction of the trends; the numbers were shown on slides the captions do not describe. The 27% usage cutoff is "arbitrary" by his own word, the group is small, and he warns that the unassisted-three rise is driven by two players and the math may be wrong (BJkCqf6Fj2w [11:47]). NBA data only. It does not show these shots are efficient; a questioner raised that and the answer was that the shot clock limits alternatives (BJkCqf6Fj2w [23:25], [23:56]).

**Example** — The talk's: 7% to 11.5% of high-usage players' made shots being long twos (BJkCqf6Fj2w [10:44]).

15:Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013. It measures cognitive ability and personality traits tied to football, and is meant as an addition to physical and film evidence. A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. The second half describes player-type clusters, a bust-rate comparison using a public value metric, and planned longitudinal modeling of second contracts.

15:Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

# Quarterback and Scheme Are Entangled With a Receiver's Open Score

**What it is** — A panelist says the team had assumed the quarterback would matter for catch score and less for YAC, while getting open would belong to the receiver, the play design and the opponent, "but what we found is that's not true" (teg9SfzpMy0 [29:25], [29:55]). To account for it they ran an adjusted plus-minus of quarterbacks and receivers across multiple seasons, using a good mix of pairings (teg9SfzpMy0 [29:55]). Their finding: quarterbacks consistently help receivers get a better open score for reasons the panel can only list (target choice, extending plays, reading the field, possibly looking off safeties). The example: Patrick Mahomes was "pretty average" on catch score once his throws were accounted for, but "blows it out of the water" on open score (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27], [30:57]). In Q&A, scheme and quarterback cannot be separated: quarterbacks stay in one scheme and the data do not allow a controlled experiment such as moving Mahomes to a different system; the model includes route and coverage context, a "sliver" of scheme, and no overall team or coach variable (teg9SfzpMy0 [51:25], [51:55], [52:25], [52:56]).

A hedged application: Seattle's receivers rated near the top with or without Russell Wilson and Denver's were last, so part of Wilson's decline could lie with the receivers; the panel says it is not claiming Wilson's decline is not his (teg9SfzpMy0 [33:59], [34:32], [35:02]).

**Why it works** — The panel's account is that the quarterback's choices change which receivers are open (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27], [30:57]). They say they cannot tell which of those it is. Inference: any receiver number is a receiver-plus-quarterback-plus-scheme number until the three can be separated by pairings or changes of team.

**When to apply** — As a standing caveat on receiver (and similar) metrics, and a reason to compare players who changed teams. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit). Inference: both warn against reading a context-free number as a player trait.

**When NOT to apply** — The panel gives no size for the quarterback effect and no adjusted values in the captions. `untested`. The Wilson story is explicitly speculative, and the panel's own wording is "maybe there's more to the story" (teg9SfzpMy0 [35:02], [35:32]). NFL tracking data with x and y only. Not applicable to college data without a similar tracking source.

**Example** — The panel's: Mahomes, average on catch score but very high on open score (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27]).

**Related** — [[claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting]], the SSAC26 talk reaches the scheme limit on the defensive side (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:43]); [[framework--open-score-orientation-speed-trajectory-before-release]]; [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]].

# In a Soccer Injury Model, Short- and Long-Term Workload and Detailed Injury History Mattered Most

**What it is** — The presenters report a gradient-boosted tree injury model (caption "XG boost") trained on injury-related features built from 2017-18 Premier League data and a historical career injury dataset (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). Inputs per player and match include workload from earlier selections, injury history (age, number of injuries) and context such as opponent and travel distance (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]). Using SHAP values, the least important group was contextual: travel to the game and rain. The next group, with somewhat more weight: days since the last injury, match-day temperature and age. The group that contributed most: the player's workload across matches, both short and long term, and the player's detailed injury history (K5a7C4b1Cwc [04:03], [04:33]). Testing: a 70/30 split with "five-block" cross-validation (caption spelling, probably five-fold), log loss 0.16, outperforming other base models tried (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42]); a Pearson correlation of 0.77 between the model's predictions and the 2018/19 Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). The talk does not say what was correlated (it reads as predicted versus observed injury outcomes) and gives no number of injuries or players.

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism for why workload and injury history dominate; they report the SHAP ranking. Inference: prior injuries and recent load are the two inputs most directly tied to a specific player's tissue state, while travel and weather are shared across a squad.

**When to apply** — As a prior for what to log first when building an injury model with limited data: workload at more than one time scale, and a detailed injury history. Eric's baseline: there is no formal injury-risk model, and movement screens are collected and filed without changing programs (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit); this model's top inputs are workload and history, not screens.

**When NOT to apply** — Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model, because tracking data is not open (K5a7C4b1Cwc [17:53]); there was no club medical data and no training load, so the workload feature misses training exposure, which a questioner pressed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:24], [18:54]). One league, two seasons, soccer, professional players. The presenter says it is a decision framework, "not an expert medical prediction model" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:54]). A correlation of 0.77 and a log loss of 0.16 are reported without class balance, so how the model would rank athletes in practice is unknown. Existing library caution: ACWR-style workload features carry the confounding concern in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]], which this model's authors do not address.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for a player facing Watford, the model takes his workload from the previous selections, his injury history and age, and the opponent and travel distance, and outputs an injury probability for that match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (workload-ratio confounding, contested). Existing library: [[research-papers/carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]].

chapter: "pcp9h_M6Ir8"
confidence: supported
# Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration

**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):

1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance".
3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.

**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.

**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; calibration of a different model: [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]] and [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]].

# A "hit count" for head impacts, modeled on baseball's pitch count

**What it is** — The speaker proposes counting head impacts the way baseball counts pitches: a cumulative exposure with a limit and rest, because subconcussive blows (hits that cause no clinical symptoms and pass the usual tests) may still injure the brain (npgdKKdJSww [15:46], [16:16]). He says the NFL let him announce the goal of a hit count at a Super Bowl press conference (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). The steps he gives:
- Model it on the pitch count: age caps (75 pitches at age 10, 85 at 11) plus mandatory rest (three days after 61 pitches). He admits those numbers are "clearly not based on much science" ("every number ends on five"), and accepts that as good enough to protect people (npgdKKdJSww [17:19]).
- Accept that low-level bumps are probably harmless, that damage is probable from some level up to concussive levels, and that the middle is unknown; lowering the number of hits lowers concussion risk too (npgdKKdJSww [17:50]).
- Count with sensors: he says college football players take "somewhere between 500 and 1,000 blows", one high school player took 2,235 blows above 10 G in 3 months, hockey players average a few hundred, and some near a thousand (npgdKKdJSww [18:20]).
- Pick a line, knowing "no one knows what that is" (npgdKKdJSww [18:20], [18:51]).
- Look by position: average force is about the same across football positions but totals differ: wide receivers under 400, linemen near or well over 1,000. An arbitrary cap of 500 would leave linemen, running backs and linebackers unable to finish a season (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]).

He also adds exposure across sports: 2,000 in football, about 1,000 in ice hockey, a couple of thousand in soccer, "probably no child" should take 5,000 head hits a year (npgdKKdJSww [20:24]), and a soccer-heading study (caption "Lipton", unpublished, diffusion tensor imaging) in which players taking up to 5,000 headers a year with over 1,300 were more likely to have cognitive and imaging abnormalities in their early 30s (npgdKKdJSww [20:55]).

**Why it works** — His analogy is that "your elbow will wear out" with too many throws and "your brain will wear out" with too many hits, with the brain more important (npgdKKdJSww [16:48]). He gives no dose-response data for the brain. Inference: the idea works as a monitoring structure (count, cap, rest) even before a safe number is known, because it makes exposure visible by position and by week.

**When to apply** — When building an exposure report by position group, where counts per athlete are the output and a cap is not yet set. Inference: a weekly count by position, shown to Athletic Medicine and the coaching staff, is the decision aid; a cap needs Baylor's own data over several seasons.

Eric's baseline: abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver and progressions are kept smooth (Inferred, transcript, speaker unconfirmed, course team position); there is no formal injury-risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12), and ACWR is looked at but not trusted ("raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context"). The course material also warns that heavy load-monitoring culture can push teams toward under-preparing athletes (Inferred, transcript, course team position); the speaker gives no evidence on that trade-off.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not set a cap from any number in the talk: the speaker says no one knows the line, the 5,000-header study is unpublished and from soccer, and the sensor counts are a few cases in football and hockey with no validity data for the devices. The talk's youth examples (Pop Warner, a high school player) do not give college thresholds. Impact sensors in 2012 recorded linear acceleration only, and the speaker says some marketing was "unethical" (npgdKKdJSww [08:04]). Using GPS-unit collision output as a head-impact proxy is an inference this talk does not support.

**Example** — The speaker's own positional comparison: receivers under 400 impacts, linemen near or over 1,000 at about the same average force (npgdKKdJSww [18:51]). The caption at [18:51] ("th000") is garbled; the figure is as read.

**Related** — [[framework--impact-alert-threshold-and-sideline-test-pairing]]; [[claim--practice-contact-is-the-largest-exposure-lever-in-football]]; [[framework--pitch-smart-count-and-rest-guideline-program]] (the baseball pitch-count program this one is modeled on, from a 2017 talk); [[claim--youth-pitching-over-100-innings-triples-serious-injury-risk]] (the exposure evidence behind pitch counts, from a 2015 talk).

# Cluster Players on Physical and Psychological Scores Together to Find Types, Not Single Scores

**What it is** — The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") argues that the psychological characteristics had been studied "really in isolation", so the next step is the multivariate profile: "different types of players who have different constellations" and how each relates to "derailment or risk factors" (40NV3_u9tYY [19:44], [20:14]). Method: cluster analysis and mixture models, borrowed from market research (profiling customers by behavior and attitude), applied to 2014 to 2016 data (40NV3_u9tYY [21:16], [21:46], [22:16]). Inputs: coach-rated physical talent plus the psychological scores, shown as z-scores (40NV3_u9tYY [22:16], [22:47]). Output: nine profiles, for example:
- Cluster 7: above average on physical and on the psychological scores, "the whole package" (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).
- Cluster 9: above average psychologically, less physically talented (40NV3_u9tYY [22:47]).
- Cluster 3: physically talented, weak on teammate, leadership, preparedness and dependability (40NV3_u9tYY [23:18]).
- Cluster 6: low on everything (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]).
He proposes tagging risk factors and success factors to each cluster and, as a risk-management idea, avoiding or "pricing in" the risk like insurance (40NV3_u9tYY [20:14], [23:18]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the claim that "there's a lot of ways to be a successful football player" (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]). Inference: clustering preserves combinations (strong body and weak habits, or the reverse) that a single composite score averages away.

**When to apply** — As a design for profiling athletes on more than one axis. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." Inference: a Baylor version would start from a decision (a recruiting, roster or development question) and then ask whether any two-axis profile informs it. The talk shows no cluster results for college athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the talk shows a model result with no validation of the clusters shown, no cluster sizes, no position breakdowns and no confidence intervals. The "physical" axis is the coaches' rating, not a measurement. The cluster count (nine) is the result of the speaker's analysis; he does not say how it was chosen. The speakers sell or run the assessment (see the criterion-validation entry). The method is described for NFL players, rookie to early career; it should not be applied to Baylor athletes without Baylor's own data and a defined outcome.

**Example** — The speaker's own comparison: cluster 3 (strong physically, weak psychologically) against cluster 9 (the reverse), described as "almost the mirror opposites" with the same failure rate (40NV3_u9tYY [25:20]; see the bust-rate entry).

**Related** — [[claim--whole-package-cluster-has-lower-bust-rate]], [[framework--criterion-validation-of-a-psychological-test-against-coach-ratings]].

# Build a Much Simpler Model Beside the Complex One as a Sanity Check

**What it is** — A panelist describes a habit: when making a complicated model from tracking data, "I'll often make a much much simpler model as a benchmark," as a sanity check that the complex one is working any better (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:18], [25:49]). In the receiver case the simple model used coverage, route, depth, play action, slot alignment and distance from the sideline to estimate catch likelihood (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49]). That benchmark turned out to be the second half of the answer to the self-created-context problem, and both were kept (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:20], [26:52]).

**Why it works** — The panelist's reason is a check: does the complicated model beat the simple one? (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49]). The panel gives no general mechanism. Inference: a simple, interpretable model sets a floor that the complex model must clear, and a gap shows what the extra complexity buys.

**When to apply** — Before presenting any composite or modeled score. Eric's baseline: a small number of valid, reliable tests is favored over an exhaustive battery (Inferred, course-team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: the same attitude toward complexity, here as a check; compare a new composite readiness or load score with one raw metric first.

**When NOT to apply** — A single reported instance, with no numbers on how much better the complex model was (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49], [26:20]). `untested`. The benchmark's variables were NFL play-level contexts; a Baylor model would need its own simple baseline. Beating a simple benchmark is not proof the complex model is valid.

**Example** — The panelist's: the simple catch-likelihood model, whose existence solved the self-created-context problem (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:20]).

**Related** — [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]], [[framework--validating-a-causal-metric-with-no-ground-truth]], a different, indirect validation route.

# Read a Linebacker Play-Action Metric as a Pair and Against Its Run-Defense Cost

**What it is** — Two cautions Eric Eager (PFF) gives in Q&A about the BDU metric.
- **Trade-off:** a questioner asks whether minimizing bite is the right objective, since it is about the mean and not the variance. Eager says a defender good at scraping down the line and stopping runs for no gain might accept giving up middle-field plays; Neville Hewitt tops the list and "maybe he is just passive," and a weaker run defense is a cost to weigh. The questioner sums it up as using analytics to "document those trade-offs and quantify them," and Eager agrees (Q3i3FOC-dPE [18:28], [18:58], [19:28], [19:58]).
- **Pair effect:** Eager calls Devin White "the interesting one" because Lavonte David, who plays next to him and whom he thinks is "considered a better player," does not do well on the metric; Eager suggests one may be the biter and the other the retreater on play action, so the team-level average of the two inside linebackers may be more informative, and the retreater may "dump value" on the metric (Q3i3FOC-dPE [24:31], [25:02], [25:32]). A questioner also notes a cornerback with a deliberate cushion would look similar (Q3i3FOC-dPE [24:01]).

**Why it works** — Eager's stated reason: the two inside linebackers in most defenses play over the guard, and one may be designated to rush toward the line because the other covers that area well (Q3i3FOC-dPE [25:02]). He offers it as a possibility ("there could be something of"), with no analysis shown. Inference: an individual metric on a position played in pairs is partly a statement about the pair.

**When to apply** — Before showing any single-player number to a position coach, ask what the player's partner and assignment are. # The same recorded action is worth different amounts depending on game state

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins argues that winning is contextual: the same action has very different value depending on game state, teammates and opponents (JjeFktc4QLM [00:00], [00:31]). His example is a made three-pointer recorded identically in the box score: in the first quarter with the team up 15 it changed win probability by 2%; in the fourth quarter of a tied game with about a minute and 30 left it changed it by 23% (JjeFktc4QLM [03:03]). He calls this a "10 times difference"; 23 divided by 2 is about 11.5, so "10 times" is approximate as spoken. He says box-score metrics such as PER and box plus-minus treat the two shots as roughly the same and so "flatten player value", making role players in blowouts look as valuable as clutch performers (JjeFktc4QLM [03:03], [03:34]). Across action types, he reports that value is highest in close clutch games, where a three-pointer can be worth "more than double" its traditional value, and shrinks in blowouts, with offensive rebounds and steals valued significantly (JjeFktc4QLM [07:39]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a point late in a close game moves the final outcome more than a point in a decided game (JjeFktc4QLM [03:34]). The 2% and 23% come from his own win-probability model; how that model was built and checked is not shown in the captions beyond the framework in [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].

**When to apply** — When a number sums events across games with very different states (grades, loads, counting stats). Inference: for football, tag snaps as close or blowout by score margin and quarter and compare a player's grade with and without the blowout snaps before using it in a playing-time or recruiting decision. Eric's baseline: no direct position (method-baseline.md has none on player-valuation or leverage-weighted models).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the 2% versus 23% is one illustrative pair of states, and the full action-value chart is described in words only. Football differs from basketball in scoring structure and win-probability models (Inference), and a Baylor-trusted football win-probability or expected-points model has not been shown. For metrics where state does not change the action's meaning (a sprint time, a force-plate jump), no leverage weighting is needed (Inference).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the first-quarter three at +15 versus the tied fourth-quarter three at 1:30, 2% against 23% (JjeFktc4QLM [03:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]], [[claim--drl-shapley-stabilizes-faster-than-rapm]].

== framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates.md
**What it is** — In catch score, a panelist describes a "catch over predicted" residual: the model predicts a catch probability, and the receiver is credited the remainder if he catches it and debited the predicted probability if not (a 0.75 prediction and a catch is credited +0.25) (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:17], [24:48]). The problem that "almost killed" the project: the receiver creates the context himself (the move that got him open), so a model that adjusts for the field at ball arrival penalizes him for making the catch easy (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:48], [25:18]). The solution, described as a "Eureka moment":
- **General context ("expected" in their words):** coverage, route, depth, play action, slot alignment and distance from the sideline (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49], [26:20]).
- **Specific context ("predicted"):** all the tracking positions at ball arrival, through a position-invariant convolutional neural network (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [26:20]).
== claim--whole-package-cluster-has-lower-bust-rate.md
**What it is** — The second speaker (caption spelling "Charles sheram") uses Pro Football Reference's "approximate value" (AV) as the outcome. A score of four or below is read as a bust, about half of drafted players; six or above is generally successful (40NV3_u9tYY [23:48], [24:19]). Reported:
- Cluster 7, "the whole package": 41% busts, so "60%" successful (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]).
- Cluster 6, "low on everything": about 83% unsuccessful (40NV3_u9tYY [24:19]). The speaker also says "0%" of this group reached the six-or-above line (40NV3_u9tYY [24:50]); the caption is unclear.

Sample: `ls | grep -v '^_' | sort | awk 'NR%3==0' | awk 'NR%4==0'` gave 12 files. I read every cited window in each `transcript.md` and checked baseline lines against `docs/method-baseline.md`.

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs transcript) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown | FIX | (1) Entry: "he was unsure of the year". Q3i3FOC-dPE [14:56]: "at the i think his pro day in 2017". The hedge is on the venue, not the year. (2) The trainers reason is labelled "Inference:", but Eager says it himself ([20:28], [20:59]). (3) Catapult as the GPS device is an Explicit baseline fact (baseline line 84), yet it sits inside an "Inference:" line. | (1) Write "at what he thinks was his pro day, 2017". (2) Make it plain text: "Eager offers one possible reason: lower picks often cannot pay trainers to optimize tests". (3) Write "Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack (Explicit)". |
| claim--decisions-under-stress-needs-ability-plus-stress-tolerance | FIX | (1) "about 0.35" is presented as clean, but the caption at 40NV3_u9tYY [15:33] reads "to about 35". The garble is not flagged. (2) The Q3 baseline quote drops its Explicit tag. | (1) Write "about 0.35 (caption 'about 35')". (2) Add "(Explicit)". |
| claim--fatigue-breaks-the-velocity-elbow-stress-link | GO | Checked: the seven-inning game and 1 to 10 rating [05:10]; "totally broke down" [05:40]; tennis, kinetic chain, planks [23:40], [24:11]; sample not stated; ODSF tag ("adopted, not Eric's own") and Inferred tag kept. | Optional: link [[claim--pitching-while-fatigued-is-the-largest-retrospective-odds]]. |
| claim--mid-range-decline-hides-steady-star-self-created-shots | FIX | (1) Entry: "340 extra unassisted threes... of which two players accounted for 308". BJkCqf6Fj2w [11:47]: "if you're looking at assisted three rates there were about 340 um extra unassisted threes... two players accounted for 308 unassisted 3es last year". "Of which" is not said, and the garble is smoothed. (2) "driven by two players": [11:16] says "a small number of players". (3) `supported` covers the whole entry, but only the share trend and the 7% to 11.5% figure ([10:44]) are stated results. | (1) Write "about 340 extra (caption 'assisted three rates', unclear), 'if I did the math correctly'; two players took 308 unassisted threes last year". (2) Write "a small number of players". (3) Scope it: "supported for the share decline and 7% to 11.5%; 340/308 untested". |
| claim--quarterback-and-scheme-entangle-with-receiver-open-score | GO | Checked: "that's not true" [29:25]; adjusted plus-minus [29:55]; Mahomes [30:27]; scheme inseparable, "sliver", no Andy Reid variable [51:55] to [52:56]; Wilson hedges [34:32], [35:02]; "a panelist" used throughout; ACWR quote Explicit. | Add a locator for "x and y only" (summary.md cites [11:24], [46:15]). |
| claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history | FIX | (1) `supported` is challenged. The claim is the SHAP ranking, a model-internal output. The 0.77 compares predictions "with reality" with no target stated (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). Workload is imputed and there are no training data ([17:53], [18:24]). The presenter disclaims "an expert medical prediction model" ([18:54]). (2) Entry: "outperforming other base models". [09:42]: "many of the other base models". | (1) Recommend `untested`: "the ranking is the model's own output; the log loss and correlation validate predictions against an unstated target". (2) Write "many of the other base models tested". |
| framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity | FIX | (1) The Nordbord baseline line drops its Explicit tag. (2) The speaker's "is not due to chance" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]) is repeated with no comment. Checked: SMD < 0.1, placebo, subsets [08:05]; "<3% variation", calibration/AUC [08:35]. `supported` is acceptable. | (1) Add "(Explicit)". (2) Add "Inference: a placebo test checks for a spurious, method-made effect, not sampling chance". |
| framework--hit-count-as-exposure-budget-modeled-on-pitch-count | FIX | (1) Entry: "Impact sensors in 2012 recorded linear acceleration only (npgdKKdJSww [08:04])". The transcript never says this: "linear" appears only at [08:35] and [16:16]. (2) The caption "a th000 on ice hockey" at [20:24] is rendered "about 1,000" with no flag. (3) "the NFL let him announce": [16:48] says "let us have the press conference". Checked: [17:19], [18:20], [18:51], [20:55] numbers. | (1) Delete the sentence, or label it Inference with a citation. (2) Write "about 1,000 (caption 'th000', unclear)". (3) Write "let his group hold". |
| framework--player-type-clusters-from-physical-and-psychological-scores | FIX | (1) The Q3 baseline quote drops its Explicit tag. (2) "The speakers sell or run the assessment" has no locator. It comes from summary.md, not from anything said aloud. Checked: [19:44] to [25:20], including nine profiles, clusters 7/9/3/6, "mirror opposites"; Charles named at handoff [19:12]. | (1) Add "(Explicit)". (2) Write "Inference (40NV3_u9tYY [00:03], a co-author 'at the NFL combine assessing the players'): the speakers run the assessment". |
| heuristic--build-a-simple-benchmark-model-beside-the-complex-one | GO | Checked: "much much simpler model as a benchmark" [25:18], [25:49]; variable list [25:49]; Eureka and combination [26:20], [26:52]; Inferred baseline tag kept. It overlaps [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]], but the benchmarking habit is a distinct angle and the two are linked. | None. |
| heuristic--read-linebacker-play-action-metrics-as-a-pair-with-run-cost | FIX | (1) "The questioner sums it up" is pinned on one person. Q3i3FOC-dPE [19:28], [19:58] has no speaker change marked. (2) "the retreater may 'dump value'": [25:32] reads "you might be valuable just because your other player can sort of... dump value". Who dumps value is unclear. | (1) Write "someone in the exchange (captions unlabelled)". (2) Quote the caption and add "(unclear which player)". |
| principle--identical-actions-carry-different-win-value-by-game-state | FIX | (1) Entry: "The 2% and 23% come from his own win-probability model". JjeFktc4QLM [03:03] gives no source. (2) "23 divided by 2 is about 11.5" is unlabelled atomizer arithmetic. (3) At [07:39], rebounds and steals are "traditionally undervalued"; the entry drops that comparison. | (1) Write "The talk does not say where the figures come from". (2) Prefix "Inference:". (3) Write "which he says traditional models undervalue". |

## Cross-entry patterns

1. **Baseline tags dropped or misplaced.** Three entries quote Explicit baseline lines without the tag, and one puts a baseline fact inside "Inference:". Grep the folder for "Eric's baseline" lines that lack "Explicit" or "Inferred".
2. **Caption garbles flagged once, then smoothed.** Entries flag one garble and clean the next ("about 35", "th000" at [20:24], "assisted three rates"). Every garbled number needs its own flag.
3. **Unlabelled connective claims.** Plausible links are written as the speaker's statements ("his own win-probability model", "sensors recorded linear acceleration only", "of which two players", "the questioner sums it up"). These are exactly the unlabelled claims the brief bans.

Dedup: I found no restatements within the folder. I grepped the SecondBrain library for elbow, concussion, pitch count, SHAP, cluster analysis, placebo, win probability, stress tolerance, benchmark and leverage. The hits are unrelated uses (joint mechanics, Myszka constraints) or research-paper briefs that the entries already link (Carey 2017). No NO-GO: every number I checked is in the transcript at or next to its locator.

## Verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** 3 GO, 9 FIX, 0 NO-GO. All fixes are text-level. One confidence change is recommended: the soccer entry from supported to untested.
